extracted.intended_audience: general readers interested in media, journalism ethics, and cultural commentary
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluation of journalistic and nonfiction-storytelling standards illustrated by This American Life's retraction of Mike Daisey's Apple exposé; focuses on distinctions between theatrical storytelling and journalistic practice, fact-checking, and corrections. Useful when judging how audio/documentary programs should handle first-person monologues and allegations about corporate practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adherence to journalistic standards
rubrics_metrics.description: "Our program adheres to the same journalistic standards as the other national shows … in this case, we did not live up to those standards."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a program operates as a journalistic enterprise, it is expected to meet mainstream journalistic standards (accuracy, verification, accountability). If an aired piece is found partially fabricated, the program should acknowledge the failure and take corrective action (e.g., retract episode, devote airtime to detailing errors).

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between theatrical tools and journalistic tools
rubrics_metrics.description: "My show is a theatrical piece whose goal is to create a human connection... It uses a combination of fact, memoir, and dramatic license to tell its story... What I do is not journalism. The tools of the theater are not the same as the tools of journalism."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Producers and contributors must recognize whether a piece is theatre or journalism. Theatrical works may legitimately use memoir and dramatic license; those techniques are not substitutes for journalistic verification. Programs should avoid presenting theatrical material as journalism without clear contextualization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accuracy/truthfulness in nonfiction storytelling
rubrics_metrics.description: Debate noted: "whether nonfiction storytellers, when they’re not calling themselves journalists, are bound to tell the truth."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nonfiction storytellers, even if working in a literary or theatrical mode, face ethical questions about factual truth—especially when claims concern real people, organizations, or serious harms. The page references discussions (e.g., John D’Agata's The Lifespan of a Fact) and examples of partly true memoirs to show this is contested; producers should decide and disclose their factual standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rigorous fact-checking process
rubrics_metrics.description: The program investigated why Daisey "misled This American Life during the fact-checking process" and referenced external reporting (Rob Schmitz for Marketplace) that "raises doubts on much of Daisey’s story."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective fact-checking must probe and verify first-person claims, especially extraordinary allegations. Editorial teams should cross-check claims with independent reporting, question narrators, and be prepared to withhold or contextualize content if verification fails. Failure of fact-checking is a core reason for retraction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency, correction, and public retraction
rubrics_metrics.description: This American Life "announced ... that it is retracting its exposé" and planned to "devote the entire hour to detailing the errors"; the episode page said: "Regrettably, we have discovered that one of our most popular episodes was partially fabricated."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When errors or fabrications are discovered, outlets should publicly acknowledge the mistake, explain what was wrong, publish corrections or retractions, and, when appropriate, dedicate coverage to separating fact from fiction. Issuing a press release and linking to investigative follow-ups (e.g., Marketplace, NYT special report) are examples of best practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate labeling and contextualization of content
rubrics_metrics.description: The piece notes the show "frequently excerpts and reproduces fictional short stories, pieces of memoir, and stories told at storytelling events," and that "perhaps different standards apply" depending on the form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors should clearly label material (fiction, memoir, reportage) and provide context for listeners/readers so expectations about accuracy are set appropriately. Reproducing theatrical or fictional material within a journalistic program requires explicit signaling to avoid misleading audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of dramatic license vs. journalistic representation
rubrics_metrics.description: Daisey: "It uses a combination of fact, memoir, and dramatic license to tell its story... I regret that I allowed THIS AMERICAN LIFE to air an excerpt from my monologue. THIS AMERICAN LIFE is essentially a journalistic ... enterprise, and as such it operates under a different set of rules and expectations."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Creators may employ dramatic license to heighten narrative impact, but when elements of a performance are presented in journalistic contexts (or as factual reportage), the use of dramatization must be scrutinized and disclosed. Editorial judgment should prevent theatrical embellishment from being mistaken for verified fact.
